title: CLAUDE.md
text: NEVER USE FIXED WEIGHTS CONTRACT QUALITY CALCULATION following approach COMPLETELY WRONG must NEVER used: - Fixed weights like .01.00 = 1.0, .03.00 = 0.8, etc. - arbitrary quality scores assigned contract types - Hardcoded quality values based contract type codes CORRECT APPROACH: Contract quality must calculated using median survival duration survival analysis: 1. Use estimate_contract_survival_optimized() function survival analysis module 2. Calculate median survival time contract type actual data 3. Convert median survival times quality scores (0.3-1.0 scale) 4. Longer median survival = higher contract quality 5. Apply employment intensity adjustments (part-time factor) data-driven approach using actual employment survival patterns scientifically sound avoids arbitrary assumptions contract quality. survival analysis methodology already implemented temporal_indicators.R module.

title: Employment Consolidation Strategies
text: Employment records administrative sources often contain fragmentation doesn’t reflect true labor market attachment. Workers may : Multiple concurrent jobs (part-time + part-time, seasonal + permanent) Brief gaps contracts (1-2 days due administrative processing) Contract renewals (employer, consecutive periods) Overlapping employment periods identified vecshift’s over_id column Without consolidation, patterns create noise longitudinal employment analysis, making difficult : Identify true employment trajectories Calculate meaningful employment durations Analyze career stability mobility Estimate transition probabilities accurately

title: Employment Consolidation Strategies
text: longworkR package provides four focused functions employment consolidation, single, clear purpose: consolidate_overlapping() - Merges concurrent employment periods consolidate_by_employer() - Merges -employer periods within gap threshold consolidate_adjacent() - Merges touching employment periods (gap) consolidate_short_gaps() - Bridges short unemployment gaps functions composable (chainable pipes) performant (9x faster previous implementations).

title: Employment Consolidation Strategies
text: Previous approach (longworkR < 0.6.0): Single function complex parameters Problems old API: - 6 different implementation files variations - Complex parameter interactions - Difficult understand consolidation performed - Performance issues large datasets - Hard compose different consolidation strategies New approach (longworkR 0.6.0+): Four focused functions Benefits new API: - ✅ Composable: Chain functions needed - ✅ Focused: function one thing well - ✅ Fast: 9x performance improvement - ✅ Clear: Intent obvious function names - ✅ Flexible: Choose consolidations apply
code: # OLD API (removed in v0.6.0) consolidated <- consolidate_employment(   data,   mode = "temporal",           # Complex parameter   type = "both",               # Complex parameter   employer_var = "employer_id", # Complex parameter   min_lag = 30                 # Complex parameter ) # NEW API (v0.6.0+) consolidated <- data |>   consolidate_overlapping() |>           # Clear: merge concurrent jobs   consolidate_by_employer("datore") |>   # Clear: merge same-employer periods   consolidate_adjacent() |>              # Clear: merge touching periods   consolidate_short_gaps(30)             # Clear: bridge 30-day gaps

title: Employment Consolidation Strategies
text: column critical understanding consolidation quality: 0 days: Truly continuous employment (gaps bridged) 1-30 days: Brief gaps, likely administrative short unemployment 31-90 days: Longer gaps, seasonal patterns search periods 90+ days: Extended unemployment bridged (use caution)

title: Employment Consolidation Strategies
text: four consolidation functions designed used sequence, creating progressive consolidation chain:
code: # RECOMMENDED: Full consolidation chain consolidated_data <- raw_data |>   consolidate_overlapping() |>           # Step 1: Merge concurrent employment   consolidate_by_employer("datore") |>   # Step 2: Merge same-employer renewals   consolidate_adjacent() |>              # Step 3: Merge touching periods   consolidate_short_gaps(30)             # Step 4: Bridge short gaps

title: Employment Consolidation Strategies
text: Always consolidate order: Overlapping first: Simplifies concurrent employment analyzing sequences Employer second: Consolidates -employer renewals employer identity still available Adjacent third: Removes administrative contract boundaries Short gaps last: aggressive, work already-simplified data Wrong order can produce suboptimal results:
code: # WRONG: Bridging gaps before merging adjacent periods wrong_order <- data |>   consolidate_short_gaps(30) |>  # Gap calculation includes noise   consolidate_adjacent()          # Less effective on noisy data  # RIGHT: Clean up first, then bridge gaps right_order <- data |>   consolidate_adjacent() |>       # Remove noise first   consolidate_short_gaps(30)      # Gap calculation more accurate

title: Employment Consolidation Strategies
text: Use data.table format: Set key better performance (optional, done automatically): Use pipe chains clarity: Consolidate analysis, :
code: # Good: data.table (fast) dt <- data.table::as.data.table(data) result <- consolidate_overlapping(dt)  # Bad: data.frame (will convert, slower) df <- as.data.frame(data) result <- consolidate_overlapping(df)  # Throws error data.table::setkey(data, cf, inizio, fine) result <- consolidate_adjacent(data)  # Slightly faster # Good: Clear pipeline result <- data |>   consolidate_overlapping() |>   consolidate_adjacent()  # Less clear: Nested calls result <- consolidate_adjacent(consolidate_overlapping(data)) # Good: Consolidate once, use many times consolidated <- data |> consolidate_overlapping() trans1 <- analyze_employment_transitions(consolidated, eval_chain = "first") trans2 <- analyze_employment_transitions(consolidated, eval_chain = "last")  # Bad: Consolidate repeatedly trans1 <- analyze_employment_transitions(   consolidate_overlapping(data), eval_chain = "first" ) trans2 <- analyze_employment_transitions(   consolidate_overlapping(data), eval_chain = "last" )

title: Impact Evaluation with Employment Metrics: A Complete Workflow
text: vignette demonstrates complete workflow integrating employment metrics calculation causal inference methods. longworkR package provides seamless pipeline raw employment data impact evaluation results three key stages: Metrics Calculation: Computing comprehensive employment metrics using calculate_comprehensive_impact_metrics() Data Integration: Preparing metrics causal analysis using prepare_metrics_for_impact_analysis() Impact Evaluation: Running causal inference methods like difference_in_differences() integrated approach allows researchers use sophisticated employment metrics outcomes rigorous causal inference studies.

title: Impact Evaluation with Employment Metrics: A Complete Workflow
text: integration metrics calculation impact evaluation follows three-step process: Integration Workflow

title: Impact Evaluation with Employment Metrics: A Complete Workflow
text: Let’s begin practical example using package’s sample employment data:
code:
# Load sample employment data from package data directory # Try multiple data file locations in order of preference data_files <- c(   "data/synthetic_sample.rds",   "data/sample.rds",    system.file("extdata", "sample.rds", package = "longworkR") )  sample_data <- NULL for (file_path in data_files) {   if (file.exists(file_path) && file.size(file_path) > 0) {     tryCatch({       sample_data <- readRDS(file_path)       cat("Successfully loaded data from:", file_path, "
")       break     }, error = function(e) {       cat("Failed to load", file_path, ":", e$message, "
")     })   } } #> Successfully loaded data from: /tmp/Rtmpr8Yddl/temp_libpath1dac209da8fa/longworkR/extdata/sample.rds  # If no data file found, create synthetic example data if (is.null(sample_data)) {   cat("No data files found, creating synthetic example data
")   set.seed(123)  # For reproducibility   sample_data <- data.table(     cf = rep(1:100, each = 4),     inizio = as.Date("2020-01-01") + sample(0:730, 400, replace = TRUE),     fine = as.Date("2020-01-01") + sample(30:800, 400, replace = TRUE),     durata = sample(30:365, 400, replace = TRUE),     over_id = rep(1:400),     prior = sample(c(0, 1), 400, replace = TRUE),     COD_TIPOLOGIA_CONTRATTUALE = sample(       c("A.03.00", "A.03.01", "C.01.00", "A.07.00"),        400, replace = TRUE     ),     event_start = as.Date("2021-06-01"),     event_end = as.Date("2021-12-31"),     retribuzione = rnorm(400, 2500, 500)   ) }  # Ensure data.table format if (!inherits(sample_data, "data.table")) {   sample_data <- as.data.table(sample_data) }  # Create event_period column if it doesn't exist if (!"event_period" %in% names(sample_data)) {   if ("event_start" %in% names(sample_data) && "event_end" %in% names(sample_data)) {     # Use event timing to create periods     sample_data[, event_period := ifelse(       fine < event_start, "pre",       ifelse(inizio > event_end, "post", "during")     )]     cat("Created event_period column from event_start/event_end
")   } else {     # Create random periods if no event timing available     set.seed(456)     sample_data[, event_period := sample(c("pre", "post"), .N, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4))]     cat("Created random event_period column
")   } } #> Created event_period column from event_start/event_end  # Examine the data structure cat("Sample data dimensions:", nrow(sample_data), "rows,", ncol(sample_data), "columns
") #> Sample data dimensions: 476400 rows, 31 columns cat("Unique individuals:", length(unique(sample_data$cf)), "
") #> Unique individuals: 4252 cat("Event periods:", paste(names(table(sample_data$event_period)), collapse = ", "), "
") #> Event periods: during, post, pre cat("Available columns:", paste(names(sample_data)[1:10], collapse = ", "), "...
") #> Available columns: id, cf, inizio, fine, arco, prior, over_id, durata, stato, qualifica ...

")    }, error = function(e) {   cat("Error in metrics calculation:", e$message, "

title: Impact Evaluation with Employment Metrics: A Complete Workflow
text: First, need define individuals treated vs. control:
code:
# Create treatment assignment # In real studies, this would come from your experimental design or policy assignment set.seed(123)  # For reproducibility unique_individuals <- unique(sample_data$cf)  treatment_data <- data.table(   cf = unique_individuals,   is_treated = rbinom(length(unique_individuals), 1, 0.4)  # 40% treatment rate )  # Add additional covariates that might affect assignment treatment_data[, `:=`(   age_group = sample(c("young", "middle", "senior"), .N, replace = TRUE),   region = sample(c("north", "center", "south"), .N, replace = TRUE),   baseline_employment = runif(.N, 0, 1) )]  cat("Treatment assignment summary:
") #> Treatment assignment summary: cat("Total individuals:", nrow(treatment_data), "
") #> Total individuals: 4252 cat("Treated:", sum(treatment_data$is_treated), "(",      round(100 * mean(treatment_data$is_treated), 1), "%)
") #> Treated: 1700 ( 40 %) cat("Control:", sum(1 - treatment_data$is_treated), "(",      round(100 * mean(1 - treatment_data$is_treated), 1), "%)
") #> Control: 2552 ( 60 %)

text: bridge function automatically detects suitable outcome variables, can also specify manually:

# Get automatically detected outcome variables with error handling available_outcomes <- character(0)  if (!is.null(did_data)) {   # Get automatically detected outcome variables   auto_outcomes <- attr(did_data, "outcome_vars")   if (!is.null(auto_outcomes) && length(auto_outcomes) > 0) {     cat("Automatically detected outcomes (", length(auto_outcomes), "):
")     cat(paste(auto_outcomes, collapse = ", "), "

")     available_outcomes <- auto_outcomes   } else {     # Manually identify numeric outcome variables     numeric_cols <- sapply(did_data, is.numeric)     exclude_cols <- c("cf", "post", "is_treated", "period")     potential_outcomes <- setdiff(names(did_data)[numeric_cols], exclude_cols)     available_outcomes <- potential_outcomes     cat("Detected potential outcome variables (", length(available_outcomes), "):
")     cat(paste(available_outcomes, collapse = ", "), "

")   }      # Select key outcomes for analysis   key_outcomes <- c(     "employment_rate",     "permanent_contract_rate",      "avg_contract_quality",     "employment_stability_index",     "transition_success_rate"   )      # Check which are available   final_outcomes <- intersect(key_outcomes, names(did_data))   if (length(final_outcomes) == 0) {     final_outcomes <- available_outcomes[1:min(2, length(available_outcomes))]   }   available_outcomes <- final_outcomes      cat("Selected outcomes for analysis:
")   cat(paste(available_outcomes, collapse = ", "), "
")      # Show descriptive statistics for selected outcomes   if (length(available_outcomes) > 0) {     tryCatch({       outcome_stats <- did_data[, lapply(.SD, function(x) {         c(Mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),            SD = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),           Min = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),           Max = max(x, na.rm = TRUE))       }), .SDcols = available_outcomes[1:min(3, length(available_outcomes))]]              print(round(outcome_stats, 3))     }, error = function(e) {       cat("Could not generate outcome statistics:", e$message, "

1.96 * std_error]           if (!"ci_upper" %in% names(plot_data)) plot_data[, ci_upper := estimate + 1.96 * std_error]         }       }     }          # Create plot if we have data     if (!is.null(plot_data) && nrow(plot_data) > 0) {       # Create coefficient plot       p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = outcome, y = estimate)) +         geom_point(size = 3, color = "blue") +         geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper),                        width = 0.2, color = "blue") +         geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +         coord_flip() +         labs(           title = "Treatment Effects on Employment Metrics",           subtitle = "Point estimates with 95% confidence intervals",           x = "Outcome Variables",           y = "Treatment Effect Estimate"         ) +         theme_minimal()              print(p)       cat("Treatment effect visualization created successfully
")     } else {       cat("No suitable data available for visualization
")     }        }, error = function(e) {     cat("Error creating visualization:", e$message, "
")     cat("Skipping visualization
")   }) } else {   cat("No DiD results available for visualization
") } #> Treatment effect visualization created successfully

# Set seed for reproducibility set.seed(42)  # Generate comprehensive employment data with multiple treatments generate_multi_treatment_data <- function(n_individuals = 2000,                                          n_time_periods = 8,                                         treatment_start_period = 4) {      cat("Generating multi-treatment employment data...
")   cat("Individuals:", n_individuals, "
")   cat("Time periods:", n_time_periods, "
")   cat("Treatment start:", treatment_start_period, "

")      # Individual-level characteristics (time-invariant)   individuals <- data.table(     cf = 1:n_individuals,     # Demographics     age = round(runif(n_individuals, 22, 55)),     gender = sample(c("M", "F"), n_individuals, replace = TRUE),     education = sample(c("basic", "secondary", "tertiary"), n_individuals,                        replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.2)),     region = sample(c("north", "center", "south", "islands"), n_individuals,                     replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.25, 0.35, 0.1)),          # Baseline employment characteristics     baseline_employment_rate = pmax(0, pmin(1, rnorm(n_individuals, 0.6, 0.3))),     baseline_wage = pmax(800, rnorm(n_individuals, 2200, 600)),     previous_unemployment_duration = pmax(0, rexp(n_individuals, 1/180)), # days     sector_experience = sample(c("manufacturing", "services", "construction", "other"),                                n_individuals, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.25, 0.45, 0.15, 0.15)),          # Unobserved heterogeneity (affects both selection and outcomes)     motivation = rnorm(n_individuals, 0, 1),     ability = rnorm(n_individuals, 0, 1),          # Network effects and regional characteristics     regional_unemployment = rnorm(n_individuals, 0.08, 0.02),     network_quality = rnorm(n_individuals, 0, 1)   )      # Treatment assignment mechanism (realistic selection process)   # Probability of treatment depends on individual characteristics   individuals[, prob_any_treatment := plogis(     -1.2 +      0.3 * (age - mean(age)) / sd(age) +  # Older individuals more likely     0.4 * (education == "basic") +        # Lower education more likely     0.5 * (baseline_employment_rate < 0.4) + # Unemployed more likely     0.3 * (previous_unemployment_duration > 365) + # Long-term unemployed     -0.2 * ability +                      # Lower ability more likely     0.1 * motivation +                    # More motivated more likely     0.2 * (regional_unemployment > 0.08)  # High unemployment regions   )]      # Assign treatments (mutually exclusive for simplicity)   individuals[, treatment_type := "control"]      # Sample treatment recipients   treatment_eligible <- which(runif(n_individuals) < individuals$prob_any_treatment)      # Among eligible, assign specific treatment types   treatment_types <- c("job_training", "wage_subsidy", "placement_assistance", "comprehensive")      for (i in treatment_eligible) {     # Conditional probabilities for different treatment types     probs <- c(       0.3,  # job_training       0.25 + 0.2 * (individuals$baseline_wage[i] < 1800), # wage_subsidy (more likely for low-wage)       0.25 + 0.15 * (individuals$sector_experience[i] == "services"), # placement_assistance       0.2 + 0.1 * (individuals$education[i] == "basic")   # comprehensive (more likely for low-educated)     )     probs <- probs / sum(probs)     individuals$treatment_type[i] <- sample(treatment_types, 1, prob = probs)   }      # Treatment intensity (for dose-response analysis)   individuals[treatment_type != "control", treatment_intensity := runif(.N, 0.3, 1.0)]   individuals[treatment_type == "control", treatment_intensity := 0]      # Treatment duration (realistic variation)   individuals[treatment_type == "job_training", treatment_duration :=                pmax(30, rnorm(.N, 180, 60))]  # 3-9 months   individuals[treatment_type == "wage_subsidy", treatment_duration :=                pmax(60, rnorm(.N, 365, 90))]  # 6-15 months   individuals[treatment_type == "placement_assistance", treatment_duration :=                pmax(14, rnorm(.N, 90, 30))]   # 2-4 months   individuals[treatment_type == "comprehensive", treatment_duration :=                pmax(90, rnorm(.N, 270, 90))]  # 6-12 months   individuals[treatment_type == "control", treatment_duration := 0]      cat("Treatment assignment summary:
")   print(table(individuals$treatment_type))   cat("
Treatment intensity by type:
")   print(individuals[treatment_type != "control",                     .(mean_intensity = mean(treatment_intensity),                      mean_duration = mean(treatment_duration)),                     by = treatment_type])      # Generate time-varying outcomes   panel_data <- data.table()      for (period in 1:n_time_periods) {          # Time period indicators     is_pre_treatment <- period < treatment_start_period     is_treatment_period <- period >= treatment_start_period     periods_since_treatment <- pmax(0, period - treatment_start_period)          period_data <- copy(individuals)     period_data[, period := period]     period_data[, post_treatment := as.numeric(is_treatment_period)]     period_data[, periods_since_treatment := periods_since_treatment]          # Generate employment outcomes with realistic dynamics          # Base employment rate (with individual fixed effects and time trends)     period_data[, base_employment := plogis(       # Individual fixed effects       -0.5 +        0.3 * (age - mean(age)) / sd(age) +       0.2 * (education == "tertiary") - 0.1 * (education == "basic") +       0.1 * ability +       0.05 * motivation +              # Time trends and regional effects         0.02 * period +  # General time trend       -regional_unemployment * 2 +              # Lagged employment (persistence)       0.6 * baseline_employment_rate +              # Random variation       rnorm(.N, 0, 0.3)     )]          # Treatment effects (realistic timing and decay)     # Job training: builds up over time, permanent gains     period_data[treatment_type == "job_training" & is_treatment_period,                  employment_effect := (                   0.15 * treatment_intensity *  # Max effect 15pp                   pmin(1, periods_since_treatment / 3) *  # Builds up over 3 periods                   (1 + 0.1 * ability)  # Heterogeneous by ability                 )]          # Wage subsidy: immediate effect, decays after treatment ends     period_data[treatment_type == "wage_subsidy" & is_treatment_period,                  employment_effect := (                   0.20 * treatment_intensity *  # Max effect 20pp                   exp(-0.1 * pmax(0, periods_since_treatment - treatment_duration/30))  # Decay after treatment                 )]          # Placement assistance: quick effect, moderate persistence     period_data[treatment_type == "placement_assistance" & is_treatment_period,                  employment_effect := (                   0.12 * treatment_intensity *  # Max effect 12pp                   (1 + 0.5 * network_quality / sd(network_quality))  # Heterogeneous by networks                 )]          # Comprehensive: large, persistent effects     period_data[treatment_type == "comprehensive" & is_treatment_period,                  employment_effect := (                   0.25 * treatment_intensity *  # Max effect 25pp                   pmin(1, periods_since_treatment / 2) *  # Builds up over 2 periods                   (1 + 0.2 * (education == "basic"))  # Larger for low-educated                 )]          # Set effect to 0 for control and pre-treatment     period_data[treatment_type == "control" | is_pre_treatment, employment_effect := 0]          # Final employment outcome     period_data[, employment_rate := pmax(0, pmin(1, base_employment + employment_effect))]          # Generate other employment outcomes     # Contract quality (0-1 scale)     period_data[, contract_quality := pmax(0, pmin(1,        0.6 + 0.3 * employment_rate + 0.2 * (education == "tertiary") +       0.1 * ability + 0.5 * employment_effect + rnorm(.N, 0, 0.2)     ))]          # Monthly wage (conditional on employment)     period_data[, monthly_wage := ifelse(employment_rate > runif(.N),       pmax(800, baseline_wage + 200 * employment_effect +             100 * (education == "tertiary") + 50 * ability + rnorm(.N, 0, 300)),       NA_real_     )]          # Employment stability (duration of current contract)     period_data[, stability_index := pmax(0, pmin(1,       0.5 + 0.4 * employment_rate + 0.2 * contract_quality +        0.3 * employment_effect + rnorm(.N, 0, 0.2)     ))]          panel_data <- rbind(panel_data, period_data)   }      # Add realistic contract type information   panel_data[, COD_TIPOLOGIA_CONTRATTUALE :=      ifelse(employment_rate > runif(.N),            sample(c("A.01.00", "A.03.00", "A.03.01", "C.01.00", "A.07.00"),                    .N, replace = TRUE,                   prob = c(0.3, 0.25, 0.15, 0.2, 0.1)),            NA_character_)]      # Create date variables   period_data[, `:=`(     inizio = as.Date("2020-01-01") + (period - 1) * 90,  # Quarterly data     fine = as.Date("2020-01-01") + period * 90 - 1,     durata = 90   )]      # Add unique identifiers   panel_data[, over_id := .I]   panel_data[, event_period := ifelse(post_treatment == 0, "pre", "post")]      cat("
Panel data structure:
")   cat("Total observations:", nrow(panel_data), "
")   cat("Individuals:", length(unique(panel_data$cf)), "
")   cat("Time periods:", length(unique(panel_data$period)), "
")   cat("Treatment types:", paste(unique(panel_data$treatment_type), collapse = ", "), "
")      return(panel_data[order(cf, period)]) }  # Generate the multi-treatment dataset employment_data <- generate_multi_treatment_data(n_individuals = 1500,                                                 n_time_periods = 8,                                                 treatment_start_period = 4) #> Generating multi-treatment employment data... #> Individuals: 1500  #> Time periods: 8  #> Treatment start: 4  #>  #> Treatment assignment summary: #>  #>        comprehensive              control         job_training  #>                  108                 1005                  119  #> placement_assistance         wage_subsidy  #>                  127                  141  #>  #> Treatment intensity by type: #>          treatment_type mean_intensity mean_duration #>                  <char>          <num>         <num> #> 1:         job_training      0.6523739     192.32671 #> 2:         wage_subsidy      0.6565235     372.06084 #> 3: placement_assistance      0.6624302      88.64191 #> 4:        comprehensive      0.6409595     272.93474 #>  #> Panel data structure: #> Total observations: 12000  #> Individuals: 1500  #> Time periods: 8  #> Treatment types: job_training, control, wage_subsidy, placement_assistance, comprehensive  # Display first few observations cat("
First few observations:

treat_pre) - (control_post - control_pre)                  manual_results[[outcome]] <- list(           did_estimate = did_estimate,           control_change = control_post - control_pre,           treatment_change = treat_post - treat_pre         )       }     }          return(list(       treatment_type = treatment_type_focus,       manual_results = manual_results,       n_treated = sum(pairwise_data$is_focal_treatment),       n_control = sum(1 - pairwise_data$is_focal_treatment)     ))   }) }  # Run pairwise analysis for each treatment type pairwise_results <- list() outcomes_to_analyze <- c("employment_rate", "contract_quality", "stability_index")  for (treatment in treatment_types) {   result <- run_pairwise_did(did_data, treatment, outcomes_to_analyze)   if (!is.null(result)) {     pairwise_results[[treatment]] <- result   } } #> Analyzing job_training vs Control: #>   Observations: 8992 #>   Treatment group size: 952 #>   Control group size: 8040 #> Analyzing wage_subsidy vs Control: #>   Observations: 9168 #>   Treatment group size: 1128 #>   Control group size: 8040 #> Analyzing placement_assistance vs Control: #>   Observations: 9056 #>   Treatment group size: 1016 #>   Control group size: 8040 #> Analyzing comprehensive vs Control: #>   Observations: 8904 #>   Treatment group size: 864 #>   Control group size: 8040  # Summarize pairwise results cat("
=== PAIRWISE DiD RESULTS SUMMARY ===

") #>  #> === PAIRWISE DiD RESULTS SUMMARY ===  pairwise_summary <- data.table()  for (treatment in names(pairwise_results)) {   result <- pairwise_results[[treatment]]      if ("results" %in% names(result) && !is.null(result$results$summary_table)) {     # Extract from longworkR results     summary_table <- result$results$summary_table     if (inherits(summary_table, "data.table") || is.data.frame(summary_table)) {       temp_summary <- as.data.table(summary_table)       temp_summary[, treatment_type := treatment]       temp_summary[, n_treated := result$n_treated]       temp_summary[, n_control := result$n_control]       pairwise_summary <- rbind(pairwise_summary, temp_summary, fill = TRUE)     }   } else if ("manual_results" %in% names(result)) {     # Extract from manual results     for (outcome in names(result$manual_results)) {       outcome_result <- result$manual_results[[outcome]]       temp_row <- data.table(         outcome = outcome,         estimate = outcome_result$did_estimate,         treatment_type = treatment,         n_treated = result$n_treated,         n_control = result$n_control       )       pairwise_summary <- rbind(pairwise_summary, temp_row, fill = TRUE)     }   } }  if (nrow(pairwise_summary) > 0) {   cat("Pairwise DiD Results:
")   print(pairwise_summary[, .(treatment_type, outcome, estimate, n_treated, n_control)])      # Create coefficient plot   if ("estimate" %in% names(pairwise_summary) && "outcome" %in% names(pairwise_summary)) {     coef_plot <- ggplot(pairwise_summary, aes(x = treatment_type, y = estimate, fill = outcome)) +       geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.8) +       geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +       scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Outcome") +       labs(         title = "Treatment-Specific DiD Estimates",         subtitle = "Pairwise comparisons vs. Control group",         x = "Treatment Type",         y = "DiD Estimate"       ) +       theme_minimal() +       theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),             legend.position = "bottom")          print(coef_plot)   } } else {   cat("No pairwise results available for summary

text: optimizes: Processing chain values like “state1->state2->state3” using eval_chain parameter analyze_employment_transitions(). problem: original implementation used sapply() strsplit(), extremely slow large datasets: solution: Vectorized string operations using sub() regular expressions: Performance impact: matters: optimization critical : - Using eval_chain = "first" eval_chain = "last" - Working transition variables contain chain histories - Processing large numbers transitions (>10,000)
code: # Original slow approach (for illustration only) process_chain_naive <- function(values, eval_chain) {   if (eval_chain == "last") {     sapply(strsplit(values, "->"), function(x) trimws(x[length(x)]))   } else if (eval_chain == "first") {     sapply(strsplit(values, "->"), function(x) trimws(x[1]))   } else {     values   } } # Optimized vectorized approach (automatically used) .process_chain_value <- function(values, eval_chain = c("last", "first", "none")) {   eval_chain <- match.arg(eval_chain)    if (is.null(values)) return(NULL)   if (length(values) == 0) return(character(0))    if (eval_chain == "none") {     return(values)   } else if (eval_chain == "last") {     # Extract everything after the last "->" (or entire string if no "->")     trimws(sub(".*->\\s*", "", values))   } else if (eval_chain == "first") {     # Extract everything before the first "->" (or entire string if no "->")     trimws(sub("\\s*->.*", "", values))   } } # Example benchmark (not run in vignette build) library(microbenchmark)  # Create test data with chains test_chains <- replicate(10000, {   n_parts <- sample(1:5, 1)   paste(sample(LETTERS, n_parts, replace = TRUE), collapse = "->") })  # Compare approaches microbenchmark(   optimized = longworkR:::.process_chain_value(test_chains, "last"),   naive = sapply(strsplit(test_chains, "->"), function(x) trimws(x[length(x)])),   times = 50 ) # Typical result: 24-49x speedup

what: 2. Weighted Median Calculation (31-59x faster, prevents memory overflow)
title: Performance Optimizations in longworkR
text: optimizes: Calculation weighted medians numeric statistics variables transition analysis. problem: original implementation used rep() expand values weights, caused memory overflow large weights: solution: Cumulative sum approach without vector expansion: Performance impact: matters: optimization critical : - Using statistics_variables numeric columns analyze_employment_transitions() - Working datasets transition weights can large (>1000) - Analyzing 50K+ observations memory efficiency crucial - Processing multiple numeric statistics variables simultaneously
code: # Original approach - DANGEROUS with large weights calculate_weighted_median_naive <- function(values, weights) {   expanded <- rep(values, times = weights)  # Can create huge vectors!   median(expanded) }  # Example that causes memory overflow: values <- c(100, 200, 300) weights <- c(1e6, 1e6, 1e6)  # Creates 3 million element vector! # median(rep(values, weights))  # Would use gigabytes of memory # Optimized approach (automatically used) .calculate_weighted_median_optimized <- function(values, weights, na.rm = TRUE) {   # Handle edge cases   if (length(values) == 0 || length(weights) == 0) return(NA_real_)   if (length(values) != length(weights)) {     stop("values and weights must have the same length")   }    # Handle NA values   if (na.rm) {     valid_idx <- !is.na(values) & !is.na(weights) & weights > 0     values <- values[valid_idx]     weights <- weights[valid_idx]   }    if (length(values) == 0 || sum(weights) == 0) return(NA_real_)    # Sort by values   order_idx <- order(values)   sorted_values <- values[order_idx]   sorted_weights <- weights[order_idx]    # Calculate cumulative weights   cumulative_weights <- cumsum(sorted_weights)   total_weight <- sum(sorted_weights)    # Find median position (50th percentile)   median_position <- total_weight / 2    # Find the value at median position   median_idx <- which(cumulative_weights >= median_position)[1]    return(sorted_values[median_idx]) } # Example benchmark library(microbenchmark)  # Create test data values <- rnorm(1000) weights <- rpois(1000, lambda = 100)  # Reasonably large weights  # The naive approach would work here but is much slower microbenchmark(   optimized = longworkR:::.calculate_weighted_median_optimized(values, weights),   naive = median(rep(values, times = weights)),   times = 100 ) # Typical result: 31-59x speedup  # Test with very large weights (naive approach would fail) large_weights <- c(1e6, 1e6, 1e6) test_values <- c(100, 200, 300)  # This works efficiently: longworkR:::.calculate_weighted_median_optimized(test_values, large_weights) # [1] 200  # This would cause memory overflow: # median(rep(test_values, large_weights))  # DON'T RUN!

code: .calculate_mode_optimized <- function(x, na.rm = TRUE) {   if (length(x) == 0) return(NA)    if (na.rm) {     x <- x[!is.na(x)]   }    if (length(x) == 0) return(NA)    # Use data.table for fast frequency counting   freq_table <- data.table(value = x)[, .N, by = value][order(-N)]    # Return most frequent value   return(freq_table$value[1]) }

code: .convert_types_optimized <- function(data, modify_in_place = FALSE) {   if (!modify_in_place) {     data <- copy(data)   }    # Find integer columns   int_cols <- names(data)[sapply(data, is.integer)]    # Convert all at once   if (length(int_cols) > 0) {     data[, (int_cols) := lapply(.SD, as.numeric), .SDcols = int_cols]   }    return(data) }

code: .normalize_transition_matrix_optimized <- function(matrix, normalize_by = "row") {   if (normalize_by == "row") {     row_sums <- rowSums(matrix)     # Avoid division by zero     row_sums[row_sums == 0] <- 1     # Vectorized division     return(matrix / row_sums)   } else {     col_sums <- colSums(matrix)     col_sums[col_sums == 0] <- 1     # Vectorized division with recycling     return(t(t(matrix) / col_sums))   } }

text: large datasets, monitor manage memory:
code: # Check available memory before analysis available_ram <- as.numeric(system("awk '/MemAvailable/ {print $2}' /proc/meminfo",                                    intern = TRUE)) cat("Available RAM:", round(available_ram / 1024^2, 1), "GB\n")  # Monitor memory during analysis library(profmem)  memory_profile <- profmem({   result <- analyze_employment_transitions(     large_dataset,     transition_variable = "contract_type",     statistics_variables = "salary"   ) })  total_allocation <- sum(memory_profile$bytes, na.rm = TRUE) cat("Peak memory allocation:",     format(structure(total_allocation, class = "object_size"), units = "MB"), "\n")  # If memory is tight, process in chunks chunk_size <- 50000 n_chunks <- ceiling(nrow(large_dataset) / chunk_size)  results_list <- list() for (i in seq_len(n_chunks)) {   start_idx <- (i - 1) * chunk_size + 1   end_idx <- min(i * chunk_size, nrow(large_dataset))    chunk_data <- large_dataset[start_idx:end_idx]   results_list[[i]] <- analyze_employment_transitions(     chunk_data,     transition_variable = "contract_type"   )    # Force garbage collection between chunks   gc() }  # Combine chunk results final_result <- rbindlist(results_list)

text: Analyzes employment transitions output process_employment_pipeline(). Identifies transitions employment periods separated unemployment periods provides transition pattern analysis. function allows specification variable use transition analysis variables compute statistics . Supports optional inline consolidation via consolidation_mode parameter, users can pre-consolidate data using composable consolidation functions (consolidate_overlapping(), consolidate_adjacent(), consolidate_short_gaps()).

title: Analyze Employment Transitions from Pipeline Output — analyze_employment_transitions
code: analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result,   transition_variable = NULL,   statistics_variables = NULL,   min_unemployment_duration = 1,   max_unemployment_duration = NULL,   consolidation_mode = "none",   consolidation_type = "both",   employer_var = NULL,   min_lag = 8,   output_transition_matrix = FALSE,   eval_chain = "last",   show_progress = TRUE )

title: Analyze Employment Transitions from Pipeline Output — analyze_employment_transitions
text: pipeline_result Output process_employment_pipeline(). Must data.table columns: cf (person identifier), arco (employment overlap count), inizio/fine (period dates), durata (period duration), optionally over_id (overlap identifier, required consolidation_mode "temporal" ""). transition_variable Character string specifying variable use transition analysis (/values). NULL (default), uses first non-standard attribute data.table. statistics_variables Character vector specifying variables compute summary statistics . NULL (default), uses non-standard attributes except transition variable. min_unemployment_duration Minimum duration (days) unemployment period consider transition (default: 1). max_unemployment_duration Maximum duration (days) unemployment period consider transition. NULL (default), upper limit applied. NULL, transitions unemployment duration min_unemployment_duration max_unemployment_duration (inclusive) included. consolidation_mode Character string specifying consolidation strategy apply transition analysis (default: "none"). Options: "none": consolidation (default, backward-compatible) "temporal": Consolidate overlapping periods using over_id "employer": Consolidate consecutive contracts employer "": Apply employer consolidation first, temporal consolidation_type Character string specifying temporal consolidation approach (default: ""). used consolidation_mode includes temporal consolidation. Options: "", "overlapping", "employment_only". employer_var Character string specifying column name containing employer identifiers. Required consolidation_mode "employer" "". Ignored modes (warning provided). min_lag Numeric value specifying maximum gap days consecutive contracts employer consolidated (default: 8). used employer-based consolidation modes. output_transition_matrix Logical. TRUE, returns square transition matrix instead normal aggregated data.table. Rows represent "" states, columns represent "" states, values transition weights (counts). Non-populated cells contain zeros. Matrix uses unique values transition_variable row/column names (default: FALSE). eval_chain Character string specifying handle chained values /columns contain "->" separators (default: "last"). Options: "last": Extract last value chains like "val1->val2->val3" (returns "val3") "first": Extract first value chains (returns "val1") "none": Leave chain values unchanged (returns "val1->val2->val3") one value ("->"), original value always used regardless parameter. show_progress Logical. TRUE (default), displays progress bar showing current processing step, percentage completion, estimated time remaining. Uses 'progress' package available, falls back utils::txtProgressBar simple messages available.

title: Analyze Employment Transitions from Pipeline Output — analyze_employment_transitions
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ library(data.table)  # Create sample employment data with transitions employment_data <- data.table(   id = 1:6,   cf = c("PERSON001", "PERSON001", "PERSON001", "PERSON002", "PERSON002", "PERSON002"),   INIZIO = as.Date(c("2023-01-01", "2023-04-01", "2023-08-01",                      "2023-02-01", "2023-06-01", "2023-10-01")),   FINE = as.Date(c("2023-02-28", "2023-05-31", "2023-12-31",                    "2023-04-30", "2023-08-31", "2023-12-31")),   prior = c(1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0),   company = c("CompanyA", "CompanyB", "CompanyC", "CompanyD", "CompanyE", "CompanyF"),   salary = c(50000, 25000, 60000, 55000, 65000, 30000) )  # Process through pipeline result <- process_employment_pipeline(   original_data = employment_data,   merge_columns = c("company", "salary") )  # Analyze company transitions with temporal consolidation transitions <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result,   transition_variable = "company",   statistics_variables = c("salary"),   consolidation_mode = "temporal",   consolidation_type = "both" )  # Compare with no consolidation transitions_original <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result,   transition_variable = "company",   statistics_variables = c("salary"),   consolidation_mode = "none" )  # Employer-based consolidation transitions_employer <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result_with_employer,   transition_variable = "company",   consolidation_mode = "employer",   employer_var = "employer_id",   min_lag = 8 )  # Sequential consolidation (both methods) transitions_both <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result_with_employer,   transition_variable = "company",   consolidation_mode = "both",   employer_var = "employer_id",   min_lag = 8,   consolidation_type = "both" )  # Analyze salary transitions with company statistics and minimum unemployment duration transitions_salary <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result,   transition_variable = "salary",   statistics_variables = c("company"),   min_unemployment_duration = 7,   show_progress = FALSE )  # Analyze transitions with duration constraints (unemployment between 7-30 days) transitions_constrained <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result,   transition_variable = "company",   min_unemployment_duration = 7,   max_unemployment_duration = 30 )  # Get transition matrix instead of data.table transition_matrix <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result,   transition_variable = "company",   output_transition_matrix = TRUE ) print(transition_matrix)  # Example using eval_chain parameter with chained values # Suppose your data has chained company transitions like "CompanyA->CompanyB->CompanyC" sample_data_chains <- copy(result) sample_data_chains[, company := ifelse(company == "CompanyA", "StartupA->CompanyA->MegaCorp", company)]  # Extract last company in chain (default behavior) transitions_last <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = sample_data_chains,   transition_variable = "company",   eval_chain = "last"  # "StartupA->CompanyA->MegaCorp" becomes "MegaCorp" )  # Extract first company in chain transitions_first <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = sample_data_chains,   transition_variable = "company",   eval_chain = "first"  # "StartupA->CompanyA->MegaCorp" becomes "StartupA" )  # Keep full chain unchanged transitions_full <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = sample_data_chains,   transition_variable = "company",   eval_chain = "none"  # Keeps "StartupA->CompanyA->MegaCorp" as is )  # ======================================================================== # CONSOLIDATION MODE EXAMPLES: Temporal vs Employer-Based # ========================================================================  # Create realistic example data with employer information result_with_employer <- copy(result) result_with_employer[, employer_id := c("ACME_CORP", "ACME_CORP", "BETA_LTD",                                        "GAMMA_INC", "GAMMA_INC", "DELTA_CO")]  # Example 1: TEMPORAL CONSOLIDATION (default behavior) # Consolidates based on over_id and time proximity, regardless of employer transitions_temporal <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result_with_employer,   transition_variable = "company",   consolidation_mode = "temporal",      # Uses over_id for consolidation   consolidation_type = "both"          # Consolidate overlapping + consecutive )  # Example 2: EMPLOYER-BASED CONSOLIDATION # Only consolidates contracts from same employer within time gap transitions_employer <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result_with_employer,   transition_variable = "company",   consolidation_mode = "employer",      # NEW: employer-based consolidation   employer_var = "employer_id",         # Column containing employer identifiers   min_lag = 8                 # Max 8-day gap for same-employer consolidation )  # Example 3: Compare consolidation approaches # Temporal: May consolidate CompanyA -> CompanyB if temporally adjacent # Employer: Never consolidates CompanyA -> CompanyB (different employers) print("Temporal consolidation results:") print(transitions_temporal) print("Employer-based consolidation results:") print(transitions_employer)  # Example 4: Stricter employer-based consolidation (7-day gap) # Useful for identifying very close contract renewals vs. true separations transitions_strict <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result_with_employer,   transition_variable = "company",   consolidation_mode = "employer",   employer_var = "employer_id",   min_lag = 7                  # Only 7-day gap allowed )  # Example 5: Permissive employer-based consolidation (90-day gap) # Useful for seasonal employers or project-based work patterns transitions_permissive <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result_with_employer,   transition_variable = "company",   consolidation_mode = "employer",   employer_var = "employer_id",   min_lag = 90                 # Allow 3-month gaps for same employer )  # Example 6: Real-world use case comparison # When you want to analyze job mobility vs. contract administration:  # For JOB MOBILITY analysis (focus on employer changes): job_mobility <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result_with_employer,   transition_variable = "employer_id",   # Analyze employer-to-employer transitions   consolidation_mode = "employer",   employer_var = "employer_id",   min_lag = 8 )  # For ROLE/POSITION analysis within and between employers: role_transitions <- analyze_employment_transitions(   pipeline_result = result_with_employer,   transition_variable = "company",       # Analyze role/position transitions   consolidation_mode = "employer",       # But respect employer boundaries   employer_var = "employer_id",   min_lag = 8 )  # Output will include columns like: # from, to (salary values for transitions) # company_from_mode, company_to_mode (company statistics) # salary_from_median, salary_to_median (if salary is in statistics_variables) } # }

title: Unified per-person career profile — career_profile
text: data data.table (vecshift_result) produced vecshift::vecshift(). Must contain least cf, inizio, fine, durata, arco, over_id, prior. indicators Character vector. indicator groups include. "core" always returned. Valid values: c("core", "stability", "complexity", "transitions", "wages", ""). "" expands four optional groups. Defaults "core". quality_source Character scalar. contract_quality computed. "survival" accepted v0.9.0; value errors message flagging reserved future-release API. reference_date Optional Date date-coercible scalar used right-censoring anchor employment_rate gap_share. Defaults max(data$fine).

title: Unified per-person career profile — career_profile
text: data.table one row per cf, keyed cf. Columns depend indicators: Core (always returned) cf Person identifier. n_periods Distinct consolidated employment periods (uniqueN(over_id[arco >= 1])). total_days_employed Total days spent arco >= 1 spells. employment_rate total_days_employed / observation_window, clamped [0, 1]. contract_quality Duration-weighted mean survival-derived quality scores per contract type (arco >= 1 rows ). intensity Duration-weighted mean prior arco >= 1. Stability ("stability" "") spell_cv Coefficient variation per-over_id total durations. gap_share Share observation window unemployment (arco == 0). max_tenure_days Longest single over_id cumulative duration. Complexity ("complexity" "") n_contract_types Number distinct contract-type codes. employer_hhi Herfindahl index employer durata-weighted shares. NA employer column detected. type_entropy Shannon entropy (natural log) contract-type duration shares. Transitions ("transitions" "") n_upward Count consecutive over_id pairs contract quality increases. n_downward Count consecutive pairs decreases. quality_slope OLS slope quality over_id rank. NA fewer two over_ids. Wages ("wages" "") wage_mean Duration-weighted mean wage. wage_median Duration-weighted median wage (via matrixStats::weightedMedian). wage_growth (last - first) / first wage computed per over_id; NA fewer two over_ids.

title: Cluster Career Trajectories into Meaningful Segments — cluster_career_trajectories
text: career_metrics data.table. Output calculate_comprehensive_career_metrics() containing career quality, stability, progression metrics n_clusters Integer NULL. Number clusters (3-6). NULL, automatically selects optimal number using hybrid method (Elbow + Silhouette). Default: NULL method Character. Clustering algorithm: "kmeans" (default), "pam", "hierarchical" features Character vector. Metric categories use: "stability", "employment", "progression", "quality", "complexity". Default: c("stability", "employment", "progression") k_selection_method Character string specifying method automatic k selection n_clusters = NULL. Options: "hybrid" (default): Uses Elbow method initial estimate, validates Silhouette micro-sample. Best balance accuracy memory efficiency. "elbow": Uses Within-cluster Sum Squares (WSS) identify "elbow" point. memory efficient, works full dataset. "silhouette": Uses Silhouette coefficient micro-sample. statistically rigorous slower. Ignored n_clusters specified manually. id_column Character. Name person identifier column. Default: "cf" min_cluster_size Integer. Minimum workers per cluster (filters small clusters). Default: 10 standardize Logical. Standardize features clustering? Default: TRUE nstart Integer. Number random starts k-means. Default: 25 seed Integer. Random seed reproducibility. Default: 123 verbose Logical. Print clustering progress? Default: FALSE use_sampling Logical NULL. Enable sampling large datasets? NULL (default), automatically enables n >= 100K. Set TRUE/FALSE override auto-detection. sample_size_k Integer. Sample size optimal k determination. Default: 50,000. Note: Automatically capped based available system memory (typically 1K-100K). sample_size_quality Integer. Sample size cluster quality metrics. Default: 50,000. Note: Automatically capped based available system memory (typically 1K-100K). batch_size Integer. Batch size distance calculations. Default: 100,000. Reduces memory spikes large datasets. memory_fraction Numeric (0-1). Fraction available RAM use distance matrix calculations. Default: 0.33 (33% available RAM). works: Function detects available (free) system RAM Calculates maximum safe sample size: max_n = sqrt(available_RAM * memory_fraction / 8 bytes) Automatically limits silhouette computation max_n observations Prevents memory overflow large datasets Recommendations: Normal use: 0.25-0.33 (balanced) Conservative: 0.10-0.20 (safer limited RAM) Aggressive: 0.40-0.50 (systems abundant RAM) Lower values reduce memory risk may limit silhouette validation sample size. experience memory errors, reduce value first.

title: Cluster Career Trajectories into Meaningful Segments — cluster_career_trajectories
text: list clustering results: cluster_assignments data.table worker-level cluster assignments labels cluster_profiles data.table cluster-level summary statistics cluster_quality list validation metrics (silhouette, Dunn, Calinski-Harabasz) feature_importance data.table feature discrimination statistics cluster_labels data.table mapping cluster IDs bilingual labels n_clusters = NULL, following diagnostic attributes attached result: wss_values Named numeric vector Within-cluster Sum Squares k tested (elbow hybrid method used). Lower values indicate tighter clusters. Names "k3", "k4", "k5", "k6". silhouette_values Named numeric vector average silhouette width k tested (silhouette hybrid method used). Range: -1 1. Values > 0.5 indicate strong cluster structure. Names "k3", "k4", "k5", "k6". k_selection_method Character string indicating method used: "hybrid", "elbow", "silhouette". decision_rule Character string describing final k chosen. Possible values: "agreement": elbow silhouette agreed k "adjacent_prefer_silhouette": Methods differed 1, silhouette chosen "disagreement_prefer_elbow": Methods differed >1, elbow chosen "elbow_only": elbow method used "silhouette_only": silhouette method used Access attributes using attr(result, "wss_values"), attr(result, "silhouette_values"), attr(result, "k_selection_method"), attr(result, "decision_rule").

title: Cluster Career Trajectories into Meaningful Segments — cluster_career_trajectories
text: Feature Selection Strategy: function uses different metric combinations based features parameter: stability: employment_stability_index, avg_employment_spell, job_turnover_rate employment: employment_rate, days_employed, unemployment_spells progression: career_advancement_index, career_success_index quality: contract_quality_score, employment_intensity_score complexity: career_complexity_index, concurrent_employment_rate Cluster Archetypes (automatically detected): Stable Full Employment: High stability + high employment rate - : "Occupazione Stabile Continuativa" Precarious Intermittent Workers: Low stability + low employment rate - : "Lavoratori Precari Intermittenti" Upward Career Progression: High advancement + increasing quality - : "Carriere Ascesa" Entry-Level Starters: Moderate quality + low advancement - : "Lavoratori Ingresso" Multi-Employment Complex: High complexity + multiple concurrent jobs - : "Carriere Multi-Impiego Complesse" Declining Trajectories: Decreasing quality + low progression - : "Traiettorie Declino"

title: Cluster Career Trajectories into Meaningful Segments — cluster_career_trajectories
text: n_clusters = NULL, function automatically determines optimal number clusters using one three methods: Hybrid Method (Recommended) hybrid approach combines two complementary techniques: Elbow Method: Computes Within-cluster Sum Squares (WSS) k 3:6 full dataset. Memory efficient (O(n*p)). Identifies "elbow" point WSS decrease rate slows . Silhouette Validation: Computes average silhouette width micro-sample (max 10,000 observations) validate elbow result. Memory bounded (O(n^2) n <= 10K). Decision Rule: methods agree -> use k differ 1 -> prefer silhouette (statistically rigorous) differ >1 -> prefer elbow (computed larger sample) Elbow Method Uses WSS analysis. Fastest memory efficient. Suitable large datasets (>100K observations) silhouette computation slow. Silhouette Method Uses average silhouette width micro-sample. accurate slower hybrid. Suitable prioritize statistical rigor speed. Memory Management function automatically limits sample size silhouette calculations prevent memory overflow: Maximum sample: 10,000 observations (hard cap) Safety factor: 0.5x theoretical memory limit 24GB RAM: typically limits ~8,000 observations ensures function can handle datasets millions observations without exceeding available memory. Scalability Large Datasets: function automatically adapts dataset size: n < 100K: Exact methods, full dataset analysis 100K ≤ n < 500K: Sample-based k determination, full clustering n ≥ 500K: Full scalable pipeline approximate metrics Important considerations large datasets (n > 100K): Use method = "kmeans" (scales millions observations) Avoid method = "hierarchical" (requires O(n²) memory, fail n > 100K) Avoid method = "pam" n > 500K (use kmeans instead) Consider specifying n_clusters directly skip k determination Increase sample_size_k better k estimates large datasets Quality metrics computed stratified samples (still accurate) Memory requirements: K-means: ~8 bytes × n × p (features) + overhead 2.7M workers × 11 features: ~240MB peak usage (manageable) Hierarchical/PAM: ~8 bytes × n² (distance matrix) - fails large n

title: Cluster Career Trajectories into Meaningful Segments — cluster_career_trajectories
text: Understanding Memory Requirements clustering function uses different memory approaches different operations: K-means clustering: O(n × p) memory - scales linearly dataset size Elbow method: O(n × p) memory - works efficiently full datasets Silhouette validation: O(n²) memory - requires distance matrix, memory-intensive Automatic Memory Management function automatically manages memory several mechanisms: Available memory detection: Detects actual free RAM (just total) Micro-sampling silhouette: Automatically limits silhouette computation memory-safe sample sizes (typically 3K-10K observations) Automatic fallback: Switches elbow-method memory insufficient Graceful degradation: Quality metrics return NA instead crashing Memory Errors Occur see "vector memory limit reached" allocation errors, try solutions order: Reduce memory_fraction (default 0.33):   Use elbow-method (fastest, silhouette):   Manually specify n_clusters (skip optimization):   Limit sample sizes (large datasets):   Close applications free system RAM Use machine RAM large datasets (>500K observations) Dataset Size Guidelines < 10K observations methods work default settings 10K - 100K observations Hybrid method recommended, automatic micro-sampling active 100K - 500K observations Hybrid elbow method, conservative memory_fraction (0.15-0.2) > 500K observations Elbow-method manually specify n_clusters Verbose Mode Debugging Enable verbose output see memory decisions:   display: Available system RAM Memory-aware sample limits Whether micro-sampling triggered Automatic fallback decisions
code: cluster_career_trajectories(   career_metrics,   memory_fraction = 0.15  # More conservative ) cluster_career_trajectories(   career_metrics,   k_selection_method = "elbow"  # Skip silhouette ) cluster_career_trajectories(   career_metrics,   n_clusters = 4  # Direct clustering, no k-selection ) cluster_career_trajectories(   career_metrics,   sample_size_k = 10000,        # Limit k-selection sample   sample_size_quality = 5000    # Limit quality metrics sample ) result <- cluster_career_trajectories(   career_metrics,   verbose = TRUE  # Shows memory limits, sample sizes, fallback decisions )

title: Compute Temporal Employment Indicators from vecshift Data — compute_temporal_employment_indicators
text: Period Calculation: Periods start reference date (default: earliest contract date). Quarterly periods span ~90 days, monthly periods ~30 days. Contracts spanning multiple periods contribute proportionally period. Consolidation: use_consolidation=TRUE, overlapping contracts over_id consolidated analysis, providing cleaner employment episode identification. Employment Rate: Calculated days_employed / period_duration, capped 1.0 periods overlapping contracts. Minimum employment threshold filters noise. Contract Quality: Calculated using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis determine median survival duration contract type. Contract types longer median survival times receive higher quality scores (0.3-1.0 scale), 1.0 represents durable contract types 0.3 least durable. empirical, data-driven approach replaces arbitrary fixed weights (e.g., permanent contracts = 1.0, temporary = 0.5) actual employment durability metrics derived survival analysis employment data . Stability Index: Combines contract duration consistency, employment continuity, transition frequency 0-1 stability measure.

Examine survival-based quality scores by contract type # This shows how different contract types are ranked by durability quality_by_type <- comprehensive_indicators[, .(   avg_quality = mean(avg_contract_quality, na.rm = TRUE),   median_quality = median(avg_contract_quality, na.rm = TRUE) ), by = contract_type][order(-avg_quality)] print(quality_by_type)  # Higher scores = more durable contract types  # Integration with impact evaluation treatment_assignment <- data.table(   cf = unique(employment_data$cf),   treatment_group = sample(c("control", "training", "subsidy"),                           length(unique(employment_data$cf)), replace = TRUE) )  indicators_with_treatment <- merge(quarterly_indicators, treatment_assignment, by = "cf")  # Difference-in-differences analysis did_analysis <- difference_in_differences(   data = indicators_with_treatment,   outcome_vars = c("employment_rate", "contract_quality", "stability_index"),   treatment_var = "treatment_group",   time_var = "period",   id_var = "cf" ) } # Must contain columns: cf, inizio, fine, durata. arco column used present identify employment vs unemployment periods. variable_handling Character string specifying aggregation strategy variables: "weight" uses weighted mean/mode (default), "first" takes first non-NA value engine Character string specifying consolidation engine: "v2" (default) uses collapse-native engine maximum performance, "v1" uses original data.table J-expression engine backward compatibility.

title: Consolidate Adjacent Employment Periods — consolidate_adjacent
text: makes periods "adjacent": Two employment periods adjacent : belong person (cf) consecutive time (gap days ) employment periods (arco > 0 missing) unemployment period unemployment acts barrier: Unemployment periods (arco == 0) prevent consolidation. example, Employment-Unemployment-Employment, consolidated even dates adjacent. Use consolidate_short_gaps want bridge unemployment gaps. Difference overlapping consolidation: consolidate_overlapping: Merges concurrent employment (over_id) consolidate_adjacent: Merges sequential employment gap Aggregation rules: consolidating periods, function: Uses min(inizio) max(fine) date range Recalculates durata full span Uses weighted mode qualitative variables (e.g., contract type) Uses weighted mean quantitative variables (e.g., salary) Weights based durata period Performance: Fully vectorized implementation exceptional performance: Handles 10M+ employment records efficiently 9x faster previous consolidation implementations (Phase 3) Phase 4 optimization: 1.2-3x additional speedup via single-period worker bypass Memory efficient: < 1x input data size Base throughput: ~41,000 records/second (Phase 3) Optimized throughput: ~50,000-120,000 records/second (Phase 4, dataset dependent) Phase 4 automatically skips consolidation single-period workers (adjacent periods possible). Performance scales percentage single-period workers: 20% singles: ~1.2x speedup 40% singles: ~1.4x speedup 50% singles: ~1.7x speedup 70% singles: ~2.9x speedup Composability: function designed chained consolidation functions: order matters: always consolidate overlapping employment first, adjacent periods, finally bridge gaps needed.
code: data |>   consolidate_overlapping() |>  # First merge concurrent   consolidate_adjacent() |>     # Then merge adjacent   consolidate_short_gaps(30)    # Finally bridge short gaps

title: Consolidate Adjacent Employment Periods — consolidate_adjacent
code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # Basic: Consolidate 3 consecutive employment periods data <- data.table::data.table(   cf = rep(1, 3),   inizio = as.Date(c("2023-01-01", "2023-02-01", "2023-03-01")),   fine = as.Date(c("2023-01-31", "2023-02-28", "2023-03-31")),   durata = c(31, 28, 31),   arco = c(1, 1, 1) )  result <- consolidate_adjacent(data) nrow(result)  # 1 (all three periods merged) result$n_periods_consolidated  # 3  # With gaps: periods separated by days won't consolidate data_with_gap <- data.table::data.table(   cf = rep(1, 3),   inizio = as.Date(c("2023-01-01", "2023-02-01", "2023-04-01")),   fine = as.Date(c("2023-01-31", "2023-02-28", "2023-04-30")),   durata = c(31, 28, 30),   arco = c(1, 1, 1) ) # Periods 1-2 are adjacent (Jan 31 → Feb 1) # Period 3 has a gap (Feb 28 → Apr 1 = 32 days)  result <- consolidate_adjacent(data_with_gap) nrow(result)  # 2 (first two merged, third separate)  # With unemployment barrier data_barrier <- data.table::data.table(   cf = rep(1, 3),   inizio = as.Date(c("2023-01-01", "2023-02-01", "2023-03-01")),   fine = as.Date(c("2023-01-31", "2023-02-28", "2023-03-31")),   durata = c(31, 28, 31),   arco = c(1, 0, 1)  # Middle period is unemployment )  result <- consolidate_adjacent(data_barrier) nrow(result)  # 3 (unemployment blocks consolidation)  # Chaining: after consolidate_overlapping() data <- readRDS("data/sample.rds") result <- data |>   consolidate_overlapping() |>   consolidate_adjacent()  cat("Original records:", nrow(data), "\n") cat("After consolidation:", nrow(result), "\n")  # Integration with transition analysis consolidated <- data |>   consolidate_overlapping() |>   consolidate_adjacent() transitions <- analyze_employment_transitions(consolidated)  # Edge case: empty data empty_data <- data.table::data.table(   cf = integer(),   inizio = as.Date(character()),   fine = as.Date(character()),   durata = integer() ) result_empty <- consolidate_adjacent(empty_data)  # Returns empty data.table  # Edge case: single record single_record <- data[1] result_single <- consolidate_adjacent(single_record)  # Returns as-is } # }

code: data |>   consolidate_overlapping() |>  # Step 1: Merge concurrent jobs   consolidate_adjacent() |>     # Step 2: Merge touching periods   consolidate_short_gaps(30)    # Step 3: Bridge short gaps

title: Consolidate Employment Periods with Short Gaps — consolidate_short_gaps
text: gaps bridged: function consolidates employment periods separated gaps max_gap_days fewer. Important: Unemployment periods duration > max_gap_days act consolidation barriers. Short unemployment periods (<= threshold) can bridged. example, max_gap_days = 30: Employment (Jan 1-15) → Gap (10 days) → Employment (Jan 26-31) = CONSOLIDATED Employment (Jan 1-15) → Gap (50 days) → Employment (Mar 6-31) = consolidated Employment (Jan 1-15) → Unemployment (20 days) → Employment = CONSOLIDATED Employment (Jan 1-15) → Unemployment (40 days) → Employment = consolidated non_working_days represents: non_working_days column tracks total unemployment days bridged within consolidated period. allows analyze "quality" employment continuity even consolidation. Use cases different thresholds: 7-14 days short breaks, sick leave, brief unemployment 30 days Monthly analysis, standard employment continuity (default) 60-90 days Seasonal work, quarterly analysis 180+ days Long-term labor market attachment Difference consolidation functions: consolidate_overlapping: Merges concurrent employment (time) consolidate_adjacent: Merges touching periods (gap, employment ) consolidate_short_gaps: Bridges short gaps brief unemployment periods; long unemployment (> threshold) acts barrier Aggregation rules: consolidating periods, function: Uses min(inizio) max(fine) date range Recalculates durata full span (including gaps) Counts total unemployment days non_working_days Uses weighted mode qualitative variables Uses weighted mean quantitative variables Weights based employment durations (unemployment excluded) Performance: Fully vectorized implementation exceptional performance: Handles 10M+ employment records efficiently Phase 5 optimization: 10-15x faster Phase 3 baseline Phase 4: Single-period worker bypass (1.2-3x additional speedup) Phase 3: Vectorized consolidation (9x faster baseline) Memory efficient: < 1x input data size Optimized throughput: ~150,000-200,000 records/second Optimization strategy: Phase 4 skips gap bridging single-period workers (gaps bridge) Phase 5 optimizes .consolidate_groups() : Splitting single-record consolidation groups (aggregation needed) Simplified first-value aggregation (avoids expensive weighted mode) Results 10-15x speedup variable_handling = "first" (default) Performance scales percentage single-period workers consolidation group sizes. function efficiently processes large-scale employment data. Composability: function designed final step consolidation chain: Always run function last, overlapping adjacent consolidation. ensures accurate gap calculations consolidation results.

title: Calculate Weighted Median Using Optimized Algorithm — .calculate_weighted_median_optimized
text: Performance Characteristics: Benchmark results show substantial improvements rep()-based approach: Speed: 31-59x faster (0.06ms vs 1.8-3.6ms 1000 observations) Memory: 96-99\ Scalability: O(n log n) complexity independent weight magnitude old approach using rep(values, times = weights) creates massive temporary vectors. example, 1,000 observations average weight 365 days (typical employment duration): Replicated vector: 365,000 elements Memory allocation: 2.92 MB per calculation Two calculations per transition (+ ): 5.84 MB 100 unique transitions: 584 MB temporary memory optimized matrixStats::weightedMedian() approach: Works directly original vectors (replication) Memory: O(n) instead O(n × w) w = average weight Numerically stable arbitrarily large weights Handles weighted median computation using efficient sorting algorithm Edge Case Handling: Empty vectors: Returns NA_real_ NA values: Returns NA_real_ Zero weights: Returns NA_real_ Mismatched lengths: Stops error Negative weights: Automatically converted absolute values matrixStats

Default: "COD_TIPOLOGIA_CONTRATTUALE" employment_intensity_var Character. Employment intensity column (1=full-time, <1=part-time). Default: "prior" employment_var Character. text: data.table contract quality metrics person period including: avg_contract_quality: Duration-weighted average quality score (0.3-1.0) total_employment_days: Total employment days period n_contracts: Number contracts period pct_permanent: Proportion time permanent contracts (.01.00) pct_full_time: Proportion time full-time employment median_survival_based_quality: Flag indicating survival-based calculation

title: Compute Contract Quality Indicators for Temporal Periods — .compute_contract_quality
text: function performs Kaplan-Meier survival analysis contract type estimate median survival times, normalizes create quality scores : Longest surviving contract types receive quality score = 1.0 Shortest surviving contract types receive quality score = 0.3 Intermediate contract types receive linearly scaled scores Unknown contract types receive default score = 0.3 Part-time contracts receive 0.8x adjustment factor Survival Analysis Method: Uses estimate_contract_survival_optimized() compute Kaplan-Meier survival curves contract type. Contracts ending maximum observation date treated censored observations. Fallback Mechanism: survival analysis fails, uses simple duration-based quality scores calculated mean contract durations type. Quality Score Range: scores bounded 0.3-1.0 ensure meaningful differentiation avoiding extreme values dominate analyses.

title: Integrated Employment Timeline and Career Metrics Visualization — plot_integrated_employment_metrics
text: employment_data data.table containing employment records processed vecshift package. Must include columns person identifiers, employment start/end dates, employment status, duration. row represents employment period individual. career_metrics Optional data.table containing career performance metrics, typically generated calculate_comprehensive_career_metrics. NULL, employment timeline displayed. Must contain person identifier column matching employment data numeric metric columns. person_ids Optional character vector specific person identifiers include visualization. NULL (default), function automatically select persons based data availability max_persons. specified, overrides automatic selection. max_persons Integer specifying maximum number individuals include using automatic person selection. Default 10. Ignored person_ids explicitly provided. Used prevent overcrowded plots large datasets. metrics_to_show Character vector specifying career metrics display right panel. Default includes four core career indices: "career_success_index", "career_advancement_index", "employment_security_index", "career_complexity_index". metrics present parameter career_metrics data displayed. timeline_width Numeric value 0 1 specifying proportion total plot width allocated employment timeline section. Default 0.7 (70% width). Must sum metrics_width 1.0 proper layout. metrics_width Numeric value 0 1 specifying proportion total plot width allocated career metrics section. Default 0.3 (30% width). Must sum timeline_width 1.0 proper layout. title Character string plot title. Default "Integrated Employment Timeline Career Metrics". Set NULL empty string suppress title. person_col Character string specifying column name containing person identifiers employment data. Default "cf" (codice fiscale). column used group records individual must match identifier column career_metrics provided. time_col Character string specifying column name containing employment period start dates employment data. Default "inizio". contain Date POSIXct values proper timeline rendering. end_col Character string specifying column name containing employment period end dates employment data. Default "fine". contain Date POSIXct values. Used calculate period durations create Gantt chart segments. status_col Character string specifying column name containing employment status information. Default "stato". Used color coding categorizing employment periods timeline visualization. duration_col Character string specifying column name containing pre-calculated period durations (typically days). Default "durata". available, durations calculated start end dates. date_breaks Character string specifying interval x-axis date breaks timeline. Default "6 months". Common values include "3 months", "1 year", "2 years" depending time span data. show_gaps Logical indicating whether display unemployment periods (gaps employment spells) timeline. Default TRUE. FALSE, active employment periods shown. palette Character string specifying color palette use employment status visualization. Default "employment". correspond predefined palettes vecshift color system. use_bw Logical indicating whether use black white color scheme instead color palette. Default FALSE. Useful publications presentations requiring monochrome output. base_size Numeric specifying base text size plot elements. Default 11. Affects titles, axis labels, legends, annotations. Larger values increase readability may require plot space. person_order Character string specifying order individuals y-axis. Options "alphabetical" (person identifier), "metrics" (career performance metrics, default), "timeline" (employment chronology). Affects visual grouping comparison similar profiles.

title: Integrated Employment Timeline and Career Metrics Visualization — plot_integrated_employment_metrics
text: function addresses common challenge employment data visualization: maintaining perfect alignment temporal employment patterns summary career metrics. Unlike approaches using separate plots faceting, single-plot solution guarantees person appears exactly y-coordinate timeline metrics sections. visualization handles missing data gracefully: career_metrics NULL, displays timeline specific metrics missing, shows available metrics warnings employment gaps exist, optionally displays distinct periods Visual encoding follows consistent conventions: Timeline uses Gantt chart representation color-coded employment status Metrics use intensity categorical encoding depending metric type Shared legend explains timeline metric encodings Consistent person ordering facilitates pattern recognition

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # ===== BASIC WORKFLOW EXAMPLE ===== # Load sample data sample_data <- readRDS(system.file("data", "sample.rds", package = "longworkR"))  # Step 1: Calculate comprehensive employment metrics metrics_result <- calculate_comprehensive_impact_metrics(   data = sample_data,   metrics = c("stability", "quality", "complexity"),   output_format = "wide" )  # Step 2: Define treatment assignment treatment_data <- data.table(   cf = unique(sample_data$cf),   is_treated = sample(c(0, 1), length(unique(sample_data$cf)), replace = TRUE),   # Add baseline covariates for matching/controls   baseline_employment = runif(length(unique(sample_data$cf))),   region = sample(c("urban", "rural"), length(unique(sample_data$cf)), replace = TRUE) )  # Step 3: Prepare for DiD analysis did_data <- prepare_metrics_for_impact_analysis(   metrics_output = metrics_result,   treatment_assignment = treatment_data,   impact_method = "did",   verbose = TRUE )  # Step 4: Run difference-in-differences did_results <- difference_in_differences(   data = did_data,   outcome_vars = c("employment_rate", "permanent_contract_rate", "career_stability_score"),   treatment_var = "is_treated",   time_var = "post",   id_var = "cf",   control_vars = c("baseline_employment") )  # ===== ADVANCED SCENARIOS =====  # Event Study Analysis # First create event time structure in original data sample_data[, event_time := ifelse(event_period == "pre", -1,                                    ifelse(event_period == "post", 1, 0))]  # Recalculate metrics with event time metrics_event <- calculate_comprehensive_impact_metrics(   data = sample_data,   metrics = "all",   period_column = "event_time" )  # Prepare for event study event_data <- prepare_metrics_for_impact_analysis(   metrics_output = metrics_event,   treatment_assignment = treatment_data,   impact_method = "event_study" )  # Multiple Treatment Groups treatment_multi <- copy(treatment_data) treatment_multi[, `:=`(   treatment_type = sample(c("none", "training", "subsidies", "both"), .N, replace = TRUE),   is_treated = as.numeric(treatment_type != "none") )]  multi_data <- prepare_metrics_for_impact_analysis(   metrics_output = metrics_result,   treatment_assignment = treatment_multi,   impact_method = "did" )  # Propensity Score Matching Setup matching_data <- prepare_metrics_for_impact_analysis(   metrics_output = metrics_result,   treatment_assignment = treatment_data,   impact_method = "matching",   outcome_vars = c("employment_rate", "contract_quality_score"),   auto_detect_outcomes = FALSE  # Specify outcomes explicitly )  # ===== DATA VALIDATION ===== # Check prepared data structure validation <- validate_integration_setup(   data = did_data,   impact_method = "did",   id_column = "cf",   verbose = TRUE )  if (validation) {   cat("Data successfully prepared for impact analysis\n") } } # }

title: RDD Placebo Tests and Density Tests — rdd_placebo_tests
text: function performs two key validity tests RDD: Placebo Tests: Estimate treatment effects alternative cutoff points true discontinuity exist. Significant effects suggest specification problems confounding factors. Density Tests: Test whether density running variable continuous cutoff. discontinuity suggests manipulation assignment variable, violating RDD assumptions. text: Problem: Unemployment periods incorrectly treated simple gaps, allowing consolidation across long unemployment spells Fix: Unemployment periods duration > max_gap_days now act consolidation barriers Impact: Short unemployment periods (≤ threshold) can bridged, long unemployment (> threshold) prevents consolidation Employment → 5-day unemployment → Employment = CONSOLIDATED ✓ Employment → 20-day unemployment → Employment = consolidated ✓ (barrier) ensures significant unemployment spells preserved consolidated career histories
